title: The Lisbon Drop
subtitle: A Novel of Wartime Lisbon
description: Lisbon, winter 1942. Neutral Portugal is a city of watchers, and Ana Ferreira is one of them — a translator in the censorship office who reads every telegram that crosses her desk. When her brother is sent to Tarrafal prison camp, Ana needs money the state will never pay. So she walks into the British embassy with copied intercepts. Then she walks to the German press office with the same pages. Both buyers are competent. Both are lying to their own services. And both believe they are her only customer. For six weeks Ana runs the simplest double game in espionage: one set of telegrams, two envelopes, a sum and a date. But a name she altered in the first sale begins to circulate in places it should never reach, and both handlers start counting discrepancies. The telegram she changed to protect her brother becomes the thread someone pulls. The ending asks one question: whose life is worth the price of a lie she already told?

editorReview.text: The Lisbon Drop excels in moral geometry, using a dual-handler structure where Ana’s lies to one handler become leverage for the other, creating a genuinely taut thriller. Her arc is visceral—moments like the release order 'pressed against her ribs' or the 'faint blue ghost' of fresh ink on her thumb ground the suspense in tangible, desperate humanity. However, the prose suffers from mechanical hiccups; repeated sentence openings and chapter-seam continuity gaps break the immersion, making the narrative feel occasionally unpolished.
